title: What to eat in Kalimpong, from cheese to churpi
meta_description: Kalimpong food explained: the Swiss-founded cheese and milk lollipops, Tibetan thukpa and shaphaley, Nepali sel roti and gundruk, churpi and the Haat Bazaar.
summary: Kalimpong's food tells its history. Tibetan traders left thukpa and shaphaley, Nepali farmers sel roti, gundruk and churpi, and a Swiss Jesuit dairy of the 1950s the cheese and milk lollipops sold in every shop. Most of it costs ₹50–250 a plate, indicative 2026, and the Haat Bazaar on Wednesday and Saturday is the place to start.

sections.heading: A trade town on a plate
paras: Kalimpong grew as a market where Tibetan wool met Indian cloth, and the people who came for that trade brought their kitchens. Tibetan families cook noodle soups, stuffed breads and dumplings. Gorkha and Nepali households, the majority in the hills, eat rice and dal with fermented greens, pickles and fried breads. Lepcha homes, the oldest in the district, ferment millet and gather forest greens. Marwari traders from Rajasthan opened sweet shops that are still in business.

The result is a town where breakfast can be sel roti and aloo dum, lunch a plate of momos, tea a slice of local cheese, and dinner a bowl of thukpa, all within ten minutes' walk of the motor stand. Prices are low, portions large, and most of the best food is in small, plain places, not hotel dining rooms.

sections.heading: Kalimpong cheese and milk lollipops
paras: The two foods most visitors carry home were started by Swiss Jesuits. In the 1950s Father André Butty, a Swiss Jesuit priest, set up a dairy in Kalimpong to give local farmers a market for their milk and taught cheese-making on the Swiss pattern. Kalimpong cheese is a mild, semi-hard round cheese with a slightly tangy taste, good with bread or on its own. The same dairy tradition produced Kalimpong's milk lollipops, soft, chewy milk sweets on a stick, sold in paper wrappers in grocery shops across town.

Both are cheap, about ₹50–100 for a small packet of lollipops and a few hundred rupees for a round of cheese, indicative 2026. Buy them from ordinary grocers near the market rather than from souvenir counters, and keep the cheese cool on the drive down. The lollipops soften in a hot car, so pack them in your cabin bag.

sections.heading: Tibetan kitchens of the bazaar
paras: The Tibetan families who settled for the wool trade, and the refugees who came after 1959, run many of the small eateries in the lanes around the market. Walk in at lunchtime and you will find steaming aluminium pots of momos, bowls of thukpa with noodles, vegetables and meat in clear broth, and thenthuk, whose flat noodles are pulled by hand and torn straight into the pot. Shaphaley, a half-moon of fried bread stuffed with spiced mince or cabbage, is the snack to take away.

Look also for laphing, cold mung-bean noodles in a sharp chilli and garlic sauce, sold by street vendors on warm afternoons, and for butter tea, salted and churned with butter, an acquired taste that makes more sense at Lava's altitude than in Kalimpong's sunshine. Pork dishes are common in Tibetan places; vegetarians should ask for vegetable or cheese momos, which nearly every kitchen makes. Prices are low, most dishes ₹60–180, indicative 2026, and service is quick.

sections.heading: The Nepali home kitchen
paras: In a village homestay you eat what a Gorkha family eats every day. Rice comes with dal, a vegetable such as squash, which grows on almost every roof and fence here, mustard greens or potatoes, and a sharp pickle of radish, tomato or the small round chilli called dalle khursani, which is very hot. Gundruk, fermented and sun-dried leafy greens, turns up as a sour soup or a pickle and is a winter staple. Kinema, fermented soybean with a strong smell and a nutty taste, is an acquired taste worth trying once.

Spring brings forest greens: ningro, the curled tips of a fern, fried with garlic, and young bamboo shoots. Many families cure meat by drying it over the kitchen fire, called sukuti, and eat it fried with onions and chilli. Ask your host what is in season. If you would like chicken or eggs, ask a day ahead; meat is often bought in Kalimpong or Lava on market days.

Mealtimes follow the farm day. Breakfast comes early, often with milky tea before anything else. Dinner is served by about 7.30 pm, and the family may eat after the guests. Join them in the kitchen if invited; sitting by the fire while rice cooks and the dog dozes under the bench is one of the best parts of a homestay.

sections.heading: Churpi, millet beer and other local tastes
paras: Churpi is the cheese of the eastern Himalaya. Soft churpi, crumbly and fresh, goes into curries and pickles with chilli and tomato. Hard churpi, smoked and dried until it is like stone, is chewed slowly for an hour or more; you will see bundles of white blocks on strings at the Haat Bazaar. Hard churpi is also sold abroad today as a dog chew.

Millet beer is the old drink of the hills. Lepcha households call it chi; Limbu families serve tongba, fermented millet in a wooden or bamboo pot topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. It is mild, warm and sour. Some homestays offer it in winter; ask politely rather than expect it, as not every family drinks. Tea, of course, is everywhere, often from nearby Darjeeling gardens, served milky and sweet unless you say otherwise.

Kalimpong district also grows ginger, large cardamom and oranges. Large cardamom, the smoky black kind, is one of the main cash crops in the forest-edge villages; you will see it drying in sheds around Kolakham and Lolegaon in autumn.

sections.heading: Eating your way through the Haat Bazaar
paras: On Wednesdays and Saturdays farmers bring their produce to the Haat Bazaar near the town centre. Come early, between 7 and 10 am, when it is busiest. This is the best place to buy edible souvenirs at fair prices and to see what the hills actually grow.
list: Soft and hard churpi, sold by weight or by the string.
Dried and pickled dalle khursani and mixed pickles in reused jars.
Large cardamom, ginger, turmeric and local black lentils.
Seasonal greens: mustard, squash tips, ningro fern in spring.
Dried fish and dried meat, for the adventurous.
Momos, sel roti and tea from stalls at the edge of the market.

sections.heading: Eating well for less
paras: Eat where the drivers and office workers eat, in the small places around the motor stand and market: thalis, momos and thukpa at local prices. Hotel restaurants charge two to three times as much for the same dishes. In the villages, take the homestay meal plan; there are few eateries, and the family's cooking is usually the best food on the trip.

Breakfast at a tea stall, sel roti, aloo dum and tea, costs under ₹100, indicative 2026. Carry a refillable bottle and ask your lodge to fill it with filtered water. Vegetarians eat well everywhere: dal, vegetables, cheese momos and paneer are easy to find, and homestays happily cook without meat if told in advance.

faqs.q: What is Kalimpong famous for in food
faqs.a: Kalimpong cheese and milk lollipops, both from a dairy tradition started by Swiss Jesuits in the 1950s, plus Tibetan dishes such as thukpa and shaphaley, Nepali sel roti, gundruk and churpi, and local ginger and cardamom. The Haat Bazaar on Wednesdays and Saturdays is the best place to see and buy local produce.

Kalimpong cheese dates to the 1950s, when Father André Butty, a Swiss Jesuit priest, set up a dairy to buy milk from local farmers and taught cheese-making on Swiss lines. The milk lollipops come from the same tradition. Today the cheese is made in small quantities and sold through grocers in Kalimpong.

faqs.q: Where can I buy Kalimpong lollipops
faqs.a: In almost any grocery shop or sweet shop around Kalimpong's market and motor stand, usually for ₹50–100 a packet, indicative 2026. They are soft, chewy milk sweets on a stick. Buy from ordinary grocers rather than souvenir counters for fair prices, and keep them out of the sun because they soften.

faqs.q: What is churpi and how do you eat it
faqs.a: Churpi is a cheese made from cow or yak milk. Soft churpi is fresh and crumbly, cooked into curries or chilli pickles. Hard churpi is smoked and dried until very hard, and you chew a small piece slowly, sometimes for an hour. Buy both at the Haat Bazaar; hard churpi travels well.

Everyday food is usually mild, with the heat on the side. Pickles made with dalle khursani, a small round local chilli, are very hot, as is the red sauce served with momos. Ask for less chilli if you prefer, and try a tiny bit of pickle before taking a spoonful. Homestay cooks adjust readily.

faqs.q: Is there vegetarian food in Kalimpong
faqs.a: Yes, plenty. Dal-bhat thalis, vegetable and cheese momos, thukpa, aloo dum, sel roti and paneer dishes are easy to find in town. Homestays cook vegetarian meals if told a day ahead. Marwari sweet shops in the bazaar serve fully vegetarian snacks. Pure vegetarians should mention that eggs and fish sauces are avoided too.

Gundruk is fermented and sun-dried leafy greens, usually mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, a staple of Nepali kitchens in the hills. It is made in autumn and early winter and stored for months. You will meet it as a sour soup with rice or as a pickle with tomato and chilli. Its tangy taste is unique.

faqs.q: Can I try millet beer in Kalimpong
faqs.a: Sometimes. Lepcha families make millet beer called chi, and Limbu families serve tongba, warm millet beer sipped through a bamboo straw. Some homestays offer it in winter, and a few local eateries sell it. Ask politely rather than expect it, since not every household drinks. It is mild but stronger than it tastes.

faqs.q: How much does food cost in Kalimpong
faqs.a: A plate of momos costs ₹60–150, a bowl of thukpa ₹80–180 and a thali ₹120–250 in local places, indicative 2026. Breakfast at a tea stall costs under ₹100. A frugal traveller eats well for ₹350–600 a day. Hotel restaurants charge two to three times as much for similar food.
